glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Solomon gathers wisdom sayings showing how a little folly spoils honor, how calm restraint helps under an angry ruler, how wisdom gives an edge in risky work, and how foolish words, careless leaders, and laziness bring ruin.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chapter 10 closes Ecclesiastes 9:1–10:20, the movement on the one event for all and on wisdom and folly. It picks up the last line of chapter 9, “one sinner destroys much good” (9:18), and shows what folly does in daily life and public life.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “If the ax is dull, And one does not sharpen the edge, Then he must use more strength; But wisdom brings success.” (Ecclesiastes 10:10)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Chapter 9 ended with a warning that one sinner can destroy much good. Ecclesiastes 10 opens with a picture of how that happens. “Dead flies putrefy the perfumer’s ointment,” and “So does a little folly to one respected for wisdom and honor” (verse 1). A reputation built over years can be spoiled by a little foolishness. The chapter that follows is a collection of short sayings, each showing folly at work in a different setting.

Some sayings concern life under rulers. When a ruler’s anger rises, the wise person stays at his post, “For conciliation pacifies great offenses” (verse 4). Solomon also sees folly raised to high places and servants riding while princes walk (verses 6–7). Other sayings concern ordinary work. Digging, quarrying, and splitting wood all carry risk, and a dull ax demands more strength, “But wisdom brings success” (verse 10). The wise person cannot remove every danger, but he works with forethought.

The chapter returns again and again to speech. “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious,” but the words of a fool “begin with foolishness,” and his talk ends in “raving madness” (verses 12–13). He multiplies words about a future no one can know. The closing sayings warn of the harm that comes to a land whose king is immature and whose princes feast in the morning, and they set beside it a land whose princes eat “For strength and not for drunkenness” (verse 17). The point is maturity and self-control, not age or rank alone. Laziness, too, lets a house leak, and the sayings end with a warning that even a curse whispered in a bedroom may be carried by “a bird of the air” (verse 20). Wisdom has real advantages, and folly, even in small amounts, does real damage.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 10:1–3 — A Little Folly Spoils Wisdom

As dead flies make perfume stink, a little folly can spoil the reputation of a person respected for wisdom and honor. The wise and the foolish differ in the direction of their hearts, and a fool shows his lack of wisdom in ordinary conduct.

Ecclesiastes 10:4–7 — Calm Before a Ruler and Honor Misplaced

When a ruler is angry, the wise person does not abandon his post, because a calm response can settle great offenses. Solomon also describes an error that comes from rulers: folly is set in great dignity while the rich sit in a lowly place, and servants ride on horses while princes walk on the ground, a picture of honor given to the wrong people.

Ecclesiastes 10:8–11 — Everyday Risks and the Advantage of Wisdom

Ordinary work carries risk, whether digging a pit, breaking through a wall, quarrying, or splitting wood, and a dull ax requires more strength while wisdom brings success. The NKJV compares a serpent that bites before it is charmed with the babbler, though some translations read the verse as a charmer who gains nothing when the snake has already bitten.

Ecclesiastes 10:12–15 — The Words and Labor of Fools

The words of the wise are gracious, but the fool is swallowed up by his own lips, and his talk moves from foolishness to raving madness. He piles up words about a future no one knows, and his labor wears him out because he cannot even find the way to the city.

Ecclesiastes 10:16–20 — Rulers, Laziness, Provision, and Careful Speech

Woe is pronounced on a land whose king is a child and whose princes feast in the morning, while a land is blessed when its king is the son of nobles and its princes eat at the proper time for strength, not drunkenness, a contrast that shows why maturity and self-control matter in leadership. Laziness lets a house decay, feasting and wine bring gladness while money supplies ordinary needs, and even private curses against the king or the rich may become known.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 10 shows how much damage a little folly can do. A careless word, a moment of rashness, or a habit of laziness can spoil years of good character. Wisdom guards ordinary conduct, speech, and work, and the chapter calls believers to take small choices seriously.

The chapter also gives practical counsel for living under imperfect leaders. Calm restraint can prevent a conflict from growing, and careful speech protects against harm. This restraint is not agreement with wrongdoing, and it does not forbid truthful accountability or seeking protection from abuse.

Finally, the sayings show both the usefulness and the limits of wisdom and money. Wisdom gives real advantage, like a sharpened ax, and money meets everyday needs (10:19). The book has already shown that money cannot satisfy those who love it or rescue anyone from death (5:10–16). These sayings describe patterns of life, not guarantees.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Folly’s outsized damage. A small amount of foolishness can spoil a good name (10:1; see 9:18).

Restraint under authority. Calm responses can quiet a ruler’s anger, even when rule is imperfect (10:4–7).

Wisdom in ordinary work. Work carries risks, but forethought and skill make effort more effective (10:8–11).

Gracious and foolish words. The words of the wise are gracious, while the fool’s talk ruins him (10:12–15, 20).

Responsible leadership and diligence. Self-indulgent leaders and laziness bring decay, while disciplined leaders bless the land (10:16–19).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Folly (10:1–3). A failure of judgment and conduct, not a lack of intelligence. The fool chooses a way that ignores wisdom and shows it in how he lives.

Right hand and left (10:2). Conventional images for the wise and foolish direction of the heart. They say nothing about which hand a person uses or about modern politics.

Conciliation (10:4). A calm, gentle response that can settle a serious offense and keep a dispute from growing.

The babbler (10:11). In the NKJV, the person whose careless talk does harm, compared with a serpent that bites before it is charmed. Other translations read the verse as a charmer who gains nothing after the snake has bitten.

Money answers everything (10:19). Most likely a practical observation that money supplies ordinary needs, including the feast and wine just mentioned. Some read it instead as the outlook of the indulgent rulers in verse 16. Either way, the book denies that money can satisfy or save (5:10–16).

A bird of the air (10:20). A picture of how words spoken in private can still become known.

focus: Ecclesiastes 10 is a collection of wisdom sayings that closes the movement begun in 9:1. Picking up the warning that “one sinner destroys much good” (9:18), it shows how folly damages a person’s honor, public order, work, speech, and leadership, while wisdom brings real though limited advantage.

sections.title: A Little Folly Spoils Wisdom
sections.summary: As dead flies make perfume give off a foul odor, “So does a little folly to one respected for wisdom and honor.” The wise and the foolish differ in the direction of their hearts, and the fool shows his folly even as he walks along the way.

sections.title: Calm Before a Ruler and Honor Misplaced
sections.summary: When a ruler’s anger rises, “Do not leave your post; For conciliation pacifies great offenses.” Solomon has also seen an error that proceeds from rulers: “Folly is set in great dignity,” while servants ride on horses and princes walk.

sections.title: Everyday Risks and the Advantage of Wisdom
sections.summary: Digging a pit, breaking through a wall, quarrying stones, and splitting wood all carry danger, and a dull ax demands more strength, “But wisdom brings success.” A serpent may bite when it is not charmed, and “The babbler is no different.”

sections.title: The Words and Labor of Fools
sections.summary: “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious,” but a fool’s talk begins in foolishness and ends in “raving madness.” He multiplies words about a future no one knows, and his labor wears him out.

sections.title: Rulers, Laziness, Provision, and Careful Speech
sections.summary: A land suffers when its princes “feast in the morning” and is blessed when they feast at the proper time, “For strength and not for drunkenness.” Laziness lets the house decay, “money answers everything,” and even a curse spoken in private may be carried by “a bird of the air.”

1.brief: Just as dead flies make perfume stink, “So does a little folly to one respected for wisdom and honor.” A small act of foolishness can spoil a reputation built over a long time.
1.explain:
Dead flies putrefy the perfumer’s ointment, gives a picture from everyday life. A few dead flies in a jar of perfumed ointment can ruin the whole batch.

And cause it to give off a foul odor; describes the result. Something precious becomes offensive.

So does a little folly to one respected for wisdom and honor. applies the picture. A small act of foolishness can spoil the reputation of a person long respected for wisdom and honor. This continues the warning of 9:18 that “one sinner destroys much good.”

2.brief: “A wise man’s heart is at his right hand, But a fool’s heart at his left.” Using the common picture of the right hand as the side of skill and favor, Solomon contrasts the wise and foolish direction of the heart.
2.explain:
A wise man’s heart is at his right hand, uses a common picture. In the ancient world the right hand was associated with skill, strength, and favor. The wise person’s heart is directed toward what is good and skillful.

But a fool’s heart at his left. contrasts the fool, whose heart is directed toward what is weak or wrong. The saying uses the conventional imagery of right and left to contrast wise and foolish orientation; it is not a comment on bodily handedness.

3.brief: Even as a fool walks along the road, his lack of sense shows, and he makes it plain to everyone that he is a fool. Folly cannot stay hidden; it reveals itself in ordinary conduct.
3.explain:
Even when a fool walks along the way, describes the fool in ordinary activity, simply walking down the road.

He lacks wisdom, says that even there his lack of sense shows. The Hebrew speaks of his lacking heart, that is, understanding.

And he shows everyone that he is a fool. says his folly is plain to all. Folly cannot stay hidden; it reveals itself in everyday behavior.
3.notes: The last line can also be read to mean that the fool calls everyone else a fool. This study follows the NKJV reading, that he reveals his own folly.

4.brief: If a ruler becomes angry with you, do not abandon your post, “For conciliation pacifies great offenses.” A calm and steady response can quiet even serious anger.
4.explain:
If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, describes a ruler becoming angry with a subordinate.

Do not leave your post; counsels against abandoning one’s position or resigning in anger. Leaving in a temper could look like guilt or defiance.

For conciliation pacifies great offenses. gives the reason. A calm, gentle response can quiet even serious anger. This counsel commends wise restraint; it does not require agreeing with wrongdoing.

5.brief: Solomon has seen an evil under the sun, an error that comes from those in authority. Rulers can make serious mistakes that disrupt the right order of things.
5.explain:
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, introduces another observation of something wrong.

As an error proceeding from the ruler: identifies the source. The evil is a mistake made by those in authority.

6.brief: Folly is set in great dignity, while the rich sit in lowly places. Misrule misplaces honor and responsibility, lifting folly up and pushing others down where they do not belong.
6.explain:
Folly is set in great dignity, describes the error. Folly itself is lifted into honor, as foolish people are given high positions.

While the rich sit in a lowly place. describes the other side of the reversal: the rich are seated low. Set beside folly raised to dignity, the picture shows the ruler’s misjudgment, an order of standing turned upside down, and verse 7 gives a second picture of the same reversal.

7.brief: Solomon has seen servants riding on horses while princes walk on the ground like servants. The usual order of society is overturned when leaders choose foolishly.
7.explain:
I have seen servants on horses, gives a picture of reversal. Horses were ridden by people of rank, yet here servants ride.

While princes walk on the ground like servants. completes the picture. Nobles walk on foot like servants. When rulers choose foolishly, the right order of society is overturned. The saying does not make rank a measure of moral worth.

8.brief: One who digs a pit may fall into it, and one who breaks through a wall may be bitten by a serpent. Ordinary work carries risks, and harmful plans can rebound on the one who makes them.
8.explain:
He who digs a pit will fall into it, warns that ordinary work carries risk, and that a pit dug to trap others can trap its maker.

And whoever breaks through a wall will be bitten by a serpent. adds another danger. Snakes often hid in the cracks of stone walls, so someone breaking through a wall might be bitten. These are observations about risk, not guarantees that every worker will be harmed.

9.brief: One who quarries stones may be hurt by them, and one who splits wood may be endangered by it. Every task carries some danger, which calls for care.
9.explain:
He who quarries stones may be hurt by them, says quarrying carries danger from falling or shifting stones.

And he who splits wood may be endangered by it. says splitting wood carries danger too, from flying chips or a slipping ax. Every task carries some risk, which calls for care and skill.

10.brief: If an ax is dull and its edge is not sharpened, more strength is needed, “But wisdom brings success.” Preparation and skill make work more effective than mere effort.
10.explain:
If the ax is dull, continues the picture of woodcutting.

And one does not sharpen the edge, describes neglecting preparation.

Then he must use more strength; gives the result. A dull tool requires more effort.

But wisdom brings success. draws the lesson. Wisdom, like a sharpened ax, makes work more effective. Preparation and skill achieve more than mere strength.
10.notes: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and translations vary in detail. The general sense, that wisdom gives an advantage over brute effort, is clear.

11.brief: A serpent may bite when it has not been charmed, and “The babbler is no different.” In the NKJV’s comparison, a person who talks without control can do harm as surely as an uncharmed snake.
11.explain:
A serpent may bite when it is not charmed; refers to snake charmers, who claimed to control serpents. A snake that has not been charmed may bite.

The babbler is no different. compares the uncontrolled talker to such a snake. In the NKJV, a person whose tongue runs freely can do as much harm as an uncharmed serpent.
11.notes: Several modern translations read the verse differently. The ESV says that if the serpent bites before it is charmed, “there is no advantage to the charmer,” and the NIV and NASB read similarly. On that reading the verse teaches that skill is useless if applied too late. The Hebrew phrase behind “the babbler” is literally “master of the tongue,” a literal gloss noted in the KJV margin, and it can describe either a charmer or a talker. This study follows the NKJV comparison with the babbler.

12.brief: “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, But the lips of a fool shall swallow him up.” Wise speech wins favor, while a fool’s own words bring him to ruin.
12.explain:
The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, says wise speech is kind, fitting, and wins favor.

But the lips of a fool shall swallow him up; says a fool’s own words destroy him. His speech becomes his ruin.

13.brief: A fool’s talk begins with foolishness and ends in “raving madness.” His speech grows worse the longer it goes on.
13.explain:
The words of his mouth begin with foolishness, describes how the fool’s talk starts.

And the end of his talk is raving madness. describes how it ends. The longer he talks, the worse it gets.

14.brief: A fool multiplies words, though no one knows what the future holds or who can tell what will come after him. He talks endlessly about matters he cannot know.
14.explain:
A fool also multiplies words. says the fool talks endlessly.

No man knows what is to be; reminds the reader that the future is unknown.

Who can tell him what will be after him? asks a question that expects no answer. The fool talks freely about things no one can know.

15.brief: The labor of fools wears them out, because they do not even know the way to the city. Their effort is wasted because they lack basic sense.
15.explain:
The labor of fools wearies them, says fools exhaust themselves with their work.

For they do not even know how to go to the city! gives the reason with a touch of irony. They lack such basic sense that they cannot find their way to town, so their effort is wasted.

16.brief: Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes feast in the morning. Immature leadership and leaders who indulge themselves bring harm to a nation.
16.explain:
Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, pronounces trouble on a land ruled by an immature king. “Child” may refer to age or to childish character.

And your princes feast in the morning! adds that its officials feast early in the day. Feasting in the morning showed self-indulgence and neglect of duty, since the morning was the time for work and judgment.

17.brief: Blessed is the land whose king is “the son of nobles” and whose princes eat at the proper time, “For strength and not for drunkenness.” In contrast to the child king and morning feasting of Ecclesiastes 10:16, such leaders show honorable, disciplined rule that serves the land rather than their own appetites.
17.explain:
Blessed are you, O land, when your king is the son of nobles, pronounces blessing on a land with a true king. The image speaks in terms of noble birth, setting such a king against the child king of verse 16, but the force of the contrast lies in how the king and his officials rule, as the next lines show.

And your princes feast at the proper time adds that its officials eat at the right time.

For strength and not for drunkenness! gives the purpose of their eating: to be strengthened for their work, not to indulge themselves. Disciplined rule serves the good of the land rather than the rulers’ appetites.

18.brief: Through laziness the building decays, and through idle hands the house leaks. Neglect brings gradual ruin, whether to a house or to a land.
18.explain:
Because of laziness the building decays, says neglect causes a building to deteriorate.

And through idleness of hands the house leaks. adds that idle hands let the roof leak. Neglect brings gradual ruin. Coming between sayings about rulers, the picture may also apply to a land neglected by its leaders.
18.notes: Flat roofs in Israel were often made of beams covered with packed earth and needed regular upkeep; without it they leaked during the rains.

19.brief: “A feast is made for laughter, And wine makes merry; But money answers everything.” Solomon observes money’s practical usefulness: it provides for ordinary needs such as food and drink, though the book elsewhere shows that money cannot satisfy or save.
19.explain:
A feast is made for laughter, says feasts are prepared for enjoyment.

And wine makes merry; adds that wine brings gladness.

But money answers everything. completes the saying. Solomon observes money’s practical usefulness: it provides the food and drink just mentioned and meets ordinary needs. Verses 16–17 have already distinguished proper feasting from indulgence, and the wider book shows that money cannot satisfy its lover or save its owner from death (5:10–16).
19.notes: Some interpreters read verse 19 as the outlook of the undisciplined rulers of verse 16, who feast for pleasure and think money solves every problem. The NKJV wording allows that reading, but this study takes money’s practical usefulness as the primary sense.

20.brief: Do not curse the king or the rich, even in your thoughts or in your bedroom, because “a bird of the air may carry your voice.” Words spoken in private can become known, so wise people guard even their private speech.
20.explain:
Do not curse the king, even in your thought; warns against speaking or even thinking contempt for the king.

Do not curse the rich, even in your bedroom; extends the warning to the powerful, even in private.

For a bird of the air may carry your voice, gives the reason with a picture. Words spoken privately can spread in unexpected ways.

And a bird in flight may tell the matter. repeats the point. What seems secret may become known, so wise people guard even their private speech.
